title: Taylor modules, initial diagrams and finite local variation
statement:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic zero. For a finitely generated $k$-algebra $A$, put $J=\ker(A\otimes_k A\to A)$ and $P^n_{A/k}=(A\otimes_k A)/J^{n+1}$, viewed as an $A$-module through the first factor. These are finite $A$-modules. At $x\in\operatorname{Spec}A$, put $t_x=\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(x)$, $h_x(n)=\operatorname{length}(A_x/\mathfrak m_x^{n+1})$ and $\Lambda f(n)=\sum_{i=0}^n f(i)$ [def-weil-pbc-module-length] [def-weil-residue-field] [def-kun-transcendence-degree]. Then
$$\dim_{\kappa(x)}(P^n_{A/k}\otimes_A\kappa(x))=(\Lambda^{t_x}h_x)(n).$$
For an etale chart $U\to\mathbf A^d_k$ in a smooth ambient scheme and a coherent ideal defining a closed subscheme $X\subset U$ [def-weil-etale-morphism] [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] [def-weil-closed-immersion] [pqf-def-coherent], for $x\in X$, Taylor expansion of that ideal at $x$ gives an ideal $K_x\subset\kappa(x)[[T_1,\ldots,T_d]]$ whose quotient by $(T)^{n+1}$ has dimension equal to this same fibre dimension. For a formal ideal $K\subset L[[T_1,\ldots,T_d]]$, order exponents first by total degree and then lexicographically, let $\mathcal N(K)$ be the exponents of first nonzero monomials of its elements, and let its vertices be the finite minimal set $V$ with $\mathcal N(K)=V+\mathbf N^d$. More explicitly, choose nonzero $G_i\in K$ representing ordered vertices $\alpha_i$ of $\mathcal N(K)$, put $E_i=(\alpha_i+\mathbf N^d)\setminus\bigcup_{j<i}(\alpha_j+\mathbf N^d)$, $\Delta_i=E_i-\alpha_i$, and $E_0=\mathbf N^d\setminus\mathcal N(K)$. Every series $F$ has a unique expression $F=\sum_iQ_iG_i+R$ with $\operatorname{supp}Q_i\subseteq\Delta_i$ and $\operatorname{supp}R\subseteq E_0$, and
$$\dim_L L[[T]]/(K+(T)^{n+1})=\#\{\alpha\notin\mathcal N(K):|\alpha|\le n\}.$$
The Taylor diagrams $\mathcal N(K_x)$ take only finitely many values locally on $U$. The set of all functions $n\mapsto\#\{\alpha\notin D:|\alpha|\le n\}$, with $D+\mathbf N^d=D$, has no infinite strictly decreasing sequence in lexicographic order. Formation of $P^n$, Taylor expansion, and these dimension identities commutes with etale localization. Adjoining $r$ free variables replaces these functions by their $r$fold iterated sums.

source.place: VIII 2.3.11--2.3.13, pp.93--94; detailed local input: Bierstone--Milman, Invent. Math. 128 (1997), 207--302, Theorem 3.17, Corollaries 3.19--3.20, Remarks 9.1, Lemma 9.3; Bierstone--Milman--Temkin, arXiv:0905.3580, sections 6.1 and 6.5. No Stacks tag states this package.

proof.text: Choose algebra generators $a_1,\ldots,a_e$ of $A$. In $A\otimes_kA$, $J$ is generated by $\delta_i=1\otimes a_i-a_i\otimes1$: modulo these differences the multiplication map is an isomorphism. As a left $A$-algebra, $P^n$ is therefore a quotient of $A[T_1,\ldots,T_e]/(T)^{n+1}$, $T_i\mapsto\delta_i$, and is spanned as an $A$-module by the finitely many monomials of degree at most $n$. This includes $n=0$ and $A=0$.

source.place: Agent-written elementary diagonal-generator calculation; compare BM Remarks 9.1, pp.275--276.

proof.text: Fix $x$, put $L=\kappa(x)$, $R=A_x$, and let $\mathfrak q=\ker(L\otimes_kA\to L)$ for $\lambda\otimes a\mapsto\lambda\bar a$. Set $S=(L\otimes_kA)_{\mathfrak q}$. Tensoring the presentation in Step 1 gives $P^n\otimes_AL=(L\otimes_kA)/\mathfrak q^{n+1}=S/(\mathfrak qS)^{n+1}$. Indeed $\mathfrak q$ is generated by $1\otimes a_i-\bar a_i\otimes1$; modulo its power every element outside $\mathfrak q$ is a nonzero scalar plus a nilpotent and has a finite geometric-series inverse. Thus localization changes no such quotient. Both $R$ and $S$ have residue field $L$. Their Noetherianity follows from finite type over a field and localization (an ideal in a localization is generated by the images of generators of its contraction).

source.place: Agent-written fibre presentation; BM Remarks 9.1, pp.275--276; Noetherian input Stacks 00FN.

proof.text: Characteristic zero makes $L/k$ separable. The smooth-subalgebra theorem writes $L$ as the fraction field of a smooth $k$-subalgebra. Base change to $R$ and localization therefore make $R\to S$ essentially smooth. The base-change and localization formulas for differentials identify $\Omega_{S/R}\otimes_SL$ with $\Omega_{L/k}$; the dimension of the latter is $t_x$. This checks the relative cotangent rank, not the dimension of the generally nonzero-transcendence-degree local ring $R$.

source.place: Stacks 037X (lemma-localization-smooth-separable), 00T4 (lemma-base-change-smooth), 00RV, 00RT and 031W and 00TV; BMT section 6.1 for the extended Hilbert--Samuel convention.

proof.text: Apply the rational-point smooth completion theorem to $R\to S$: its residue map is the identity, its rings are Noetherian, and its relative cotangent rank is $t_x$ by Step 3. It gives $\operatorname{gr}_{\mathfrak qS}S\simeq(\operatorname{gr}_{\mathfrak m_x}R)[Z_1,\ldots,Z_{t_x}]$, with degree-one variables. Write $g(j)=\dim_L\mathfrak m_x^j/\mathfrak m_x^{j+1}$. Additivity of length along the finite maximal-ideal filtration gives $h_x(n)=\sum_{j\leq n}g(j)$: every graded piece is annihilated by $\mathfrak m_x$, so a vector-space flag is a composition series. The same calculation in $S$, followed by grouping its polynomial monomials by exponents, gives $\operatorname{length}_S(S/\mathfrak q^{n+1}S)=\sum_{\beta\in\mathbf N^{t_x},\,|\beta|\leq n}h_x(n-|\beta|)=\Lambda^{t_x}h_x(n)$. Its left side is the $L$-dimension in Step 2. Each extra variable sums the previous function from $0$ to $n$; when $t_x=0$ the formula is $h_x$.

source.place: Rational smooth completion from Stacks 054L and 0AGX; length additivity 00IV; BM Remarks 9.1 and BMT sections 6.1, 6.5. The displayed monomial summation is written out by Q71.

proof.text: On an affine etale chart $\operatorname{Spec}B\to\mathbf A^d_k$ with coordinates $u_i$, write $X=\operatorname{Spec}(B/I)$ and $L=\kappa(x)$ for $x\in X$. Flatness and unramifiedness give unique lifts of $B\to L$ to $L[T]/(T)^{n+1}$ over $k[u]$, with $u_i\mapsto u_i(x)+T_i$, by successive square-zero thickenings. Set $C_n=(L\otimes_kB)/\mathfrak q^{n+1}$, where $\mathfrak q$ is the evaluation kernel. The map $L[T]/(T)^{n+1}\to C_n$ sends $T_i$ to $1\otimes u_i-u_i(x)$, and the lifted Taylor map gives a reverse map. Their composite on the polynomial algebra fixes every $T_i$; the other composite fixes the left $L$ and is the identity on $B$ by uniqueness of the lift of $B\to L$ over $k[u]$ into $C_n$. Thus they are inverse. Passing to inverse limits defines $\tau_x:B\to L[[T]]$ and the completed-diagonal isomorphism. Quotienting $C_n$ by the image of $I$ now gives $L[[T]]/(K_x+(T)^{n+1})=P^n_{(B/I)/k}\otimes_{B/I}L$, with $K_x=(\tau_x(I))$. This uses the scalar-extended diagonal, without assuming a coefficient-field section into $\widehat{\mathcal O}_{X,x}$.

source.place: Stacks 04FF (lemma-unramified-flat-formally-etale); BM Remarks 9.1; BMT sections 6.1 and 6.5. Agent-written completed-diagonal realization at nonclosed points.

proof.text: For a formal ideal $K$, exclude zero when taking first exponents. Multiplication by $T^\beta$ shows $D=\mathcal N(K)$ is upward closed. Its coordinatewise minimal elements form an antichain and hence are finite by Dickson. Every $\alpha\in D$ dominates a minimal element: choose a minimal element of the finite nonempty set $D\cap\prod_j[0,\alpha_j]$. Thus $D=V+\mathbf N^d$, and every generating subset contains $V$, proving its uniqueness. Select $G_i\in K$ with initial exponent the ordered vertex $\alpha_i$ and normalize its leading coefficient to $1$. Define $E_i,\Delta_i,E_0$ as in the statement. These disjoint sets partition the exponent tuples. Lean implementation: multiply a representative by the monomial with coefficient 1, use the shifted-coefficient formula and translation cancellation in DegLex, and apply Finsupp.wellQuasiOrderedLE to the antichain of coordinatewise minimal elements. Enumerate that finite set using Finset.orderEmbOfFin in the DegLex type synonym. Well-founded coordinatewise minimization below each exponent proves equality with generated.

source.place: BM section 3, diagram discussion preceding Corollary 3.19, pp.238--239; finite-antichain input Mathlib.Order.WellQuasiOrder.

proof.text: Apply the existing supported formal division theorem [lem-trf-supported-formal-division] to the given series G_i and their first exponents. The minimal-vertex characterization, Dickson well-foundedness, and upward closure from Step 6 identify the generated orthants with the initial diagram. Convert Function.support inclusions into HilbertCoefficient.supported. The theorem gives existence and uniqueness of both quotients and remainder, hence of their pair. Its degree estimates remain available for later uses; no new division construction is introduced here.

source.place: Agent-written coefficient-recursion proof of BM Theorem 3.17 and Remark 3.18, p.238; no division theorem is moved into a new node.

proof.text: Specialize the proved coefficient criterion [lem-weil-pbc-power-series-combined-ideal-coefficients] to the zero coefficient ideal: membership in the q-th variable-ideal power is exactly coefficient vanishing below total degree q. Let E consist of exponents outside the initial diagram of degree at most n; it is finite. Extend a coefficient function E -> L by zero to a formal series and then take its quotient class. This is an L-linear map. To prove injectivity, write a series in its kernel as k+v with k in K and v in the (n+1)-st variable-ideal power. If the extended series is nonzero, choose its first degree-lex exponent a using well-foundedness. It is in E. Since smaller degree-lex exponents have degree at most degree(a) <= n, the coefficients of v vanish there and at a; therefore a is also the first exponent of k. This puts a in the initial diagram, contrary to a in E. To prove surjectivity, choose representatives G_i of the finitely many vertices from Step 6 and divide an arbitrary representative F by [lem-trf-supported-formal-division]. Its remainder is supported outside the diagram. Truncating that remainder to E changes it by a series whose coefficients below n+1 vanish, hence by an element of the variable-ideal power. The sum of divisor multiples belongs to K, so the truncated remainder represents F in the quotient. This constructs a linear equivalence from E -> L onto the quotient. Transport module finiteness and finrank along it and identify Fintype.card E with E.ncard. The proof covers empty E, no vertices, and no variables.

source.place: Agent-written deduction of BM Corollaries 3.19--3.20, pp.238--239, from Steps 6--7.

proof.text: Work on an affine chart with generators $f_1,\ldots,f_v$ of $I$. Apply the cited calculus theorem with $r=0$, $N=U$, $w=u$. Its centered Taylor map equals Step 5's map: both send $u_i$ to $u_i(x)+T_i$, and unique lifting identifies them modulo every $(T)^q$. Coordinate derivatives $D_i$ preserve regular functions and commute with this map. Differentiating and taking constant terms gives $[T^\alpha]\tau_x(f)=D^\alpha f(x)/\alpha!$; characteristic zero makes the denominator invertible. For a degree-lex exponent $a$, discard monomials greater than $a$ and form the finite matrix of $T^\beta\tau(f_j)$ for $\beta\leq a$. Its entries are therefore regular. Steps 7--8 apply to this monomial-prefix tail since subtraction increases exponents. The specialized cokernel has dimension $c_{D_x}(a)=\#\{\gamma\leq a:\gamma\notin D_x\}$. Thus $\{x:c_{D_x}(a)\leq r\}$ is open, given by nonvanishing minors of size $N-r$, where $N$ is the number of retained monomials. Order diagrams by their increasing vertex lists padded with $\infty$; equivalently, the diagram containing the first differing exponent is smaller. For a fixed nonempty diagram $E$, let $a$ be its largest vertex. Comparing $D$ with $E$ uses only $(c_D(\beta))_{\beta\leq a}$ lexicographically: a first difference decides the comparison; agreement forces all vertices of $E$ into $D$, hence $E\subseteq D$ and $D\leq E$. A bounded integer-vector lexicographic sublevel is a finite union of coordinatewise sublevels, so $\{x:D_x\leq E\}$ is open by the minors argument. For empty $E$ it is the whole chart. The zero and unit ideals are included.

source.place: BM Remarks 9.1 and proof of Lemma 9.3, pp.275--277; current implicit-coordinate statement, r=0, with its centered map defined by completion at the residue-field-rational point. Unique lifting from Step 5 identifies the maps; derivative commutation gives the displayed coefficient formula.

proof.text: There cannot be an infinite strictly decreasing sequence of diagrams in this order. In such a sequence, for each successive exponent the membership bit eventually stabilizes: after earlier bits stabilize, the current bit can change only from absence to presence. Let $D_\infty$ be the eventual-membership diagram; it is upward closed. Step 6 applies to it, so it has finitely many vertices. At a sufficiently late index $i$, every one of these vertices belongs to $D_i$, hence $D_\infty\subseteq D_i$. But a strictly decreasing sequence converging on every finite prefix has $D_i>D_\infty$ at every index: its first later change places a monomial in the limiting diagram. Inclusion gives the opposite inequality. This contradiction also covers an empty limiting diagram.

source.place: Agent-written finite-prefix and finite-vertex proof of the diagram descending-chain assertion used before BM Lemma 9.3.

proof.text: Restrict to an affine part of the chart. Its coordinate ring is a finite-type algebra over $k$ and hence is Noetherian; its spectrum is a Noetherian space. If infinitely many diagram values occurred, the well-order property from Step 10 would give strictly increasing values $E_1<E_2<\cdots$ in that image (successively take the least remaining value). The closed subsets $\{x:D_x>E_i\}$ would then be strictly decreasing: a point with value $E_{i+1}$ belongs to the $i$th and not the $(i+1)$st set. Step 9 proves closedness, and Noetherianity prohibits this sequence. Thus there are only finitely many values on that affine neighbourhood, as asserted locally on $U$.

source.place: BM Lemma 9.3(2), pp.276--277; algebraic Noetherian inputs Stacks 00FN and 00FM.

proof.text: Now suppose $H_{D_i}(n)=\#\{\alpha\notin D_i:|\alpha|\leq n\}$ strictly decreases lexicographically. For each $n$, its value eventually stabilizes: once values at smaller arguments have stabilized, a strict lexicographic decrease can only lower the $n$th natural number or leave it unchanged. Call the limit $H(n)$. There are finitely many possible membership patterns in each degree ball. Choose a subsequence with a fixed pattern in degree at most $0$, then a subsequence with a fixed pattern in degree at most $1$, and so on, always retaining infinitely many indices; selecting increasing indices from these nested subsequences gives diagrams converging on every degree ball. Their eventual-membership set $D$ is upward closed, and its counting function is $H$. By Dickson, $D$ just constructed has finitely many vertices; all belong to every sufficiently late diagram of the chosen subsequence. Hence $D\subseteq D_i$ there and $H_{D_i}(n)\leq H(n)$ for every $n$. On the other hand every term of a strictly decreasing lexicographic sequence with stabilized finite prefixes is strictly larger than its limiting sequence: take the first argument where it differs from a later smaller term and then stabilize that finite prefix. This contradicts the pointwise inequality. Therefore the Hilbert functions have no infinite strict lexicographic decrease. This proof does not identify the order of diagrams with the order of degree-counting functions, which need not agree.

source.place: Agent-written diagonal finite-set argument for the Hilbert-function descending-chain claim; uses the finite-vertex setting of BM section 3, not a claimed monotonicity between arbitrary Hilbert and vertex orders.; Dickson finite-vertex argument as in Step 6.

proof.text: For an etale map $A\to A'$, formal etaleness gives a unique extension of the right $A$-map to a right $A'$-map on each nilpotent diagonal thickening of $A'\otimes_AP^n_{A/k}$, reducing modulo the diagonal ideal to the identity on $A'$. The two maps given by this lift and by the universal tensor generators are inverse, by uniqueness at every square-zero stage. Thus $A'\otimes_AP^n_{A/k}\simeq P^n_{A'/k}$. At a point $x'$ above $x$ this identifies the fibres after scalar extension $\kappa(x)\to\kappa(x')$. The same unique lifts define the Taylor maps in Step 5, so their diagrams and all finite-dimensional truncations agree after that field extension. Scalar extension preserves the rank of each finite matrix (a minor vanishes or does not vanish in either field); Steps 8--9 give equality of the stated dimensions. Ordinary open localizations are included.

source.place: Stacks 04FF and the defining diagonal presentation; agent-written compatibility proof. Compare BM Remarks 9.1 and BMT section 6.5.

proof.text: Finally extend $K\subset L[[T]]$ to $L[[T,Z_1,\ldots,Z_r]]$ without adding equations. Expanding in the $Z$ monomials shows that its initial diagram is $D\times\mathbf N^r$: a leading coefficient in $T$ of any nonzero $Z$ coefficient lies in $D$, and monomial multiples of vertex representatives give every element of that product. The complement is $(\mathbf N^d\setminus D)\times\mathbf N^r$. In total degree at most $n$, grouping by the last exponent gives $H_{D\times\mathbf N}(n)=\sum_{j=0}^nH_D(n-j)$; repeating this for each new variable gives $\Lambda^rH_D(n)$. This includes $r=0$, $d=0$, $K=0$, and $K=(1)$.

source.place: Agent-written monomial count, matching BMT section 6.5, product-diagram observation.
